body.text: Walkways take more abuse than they get credit for

Front walkways and garden paths get walked, shovelled, salted and rained on more consistently than almost any other concrete on a property, yet they are often the last surface homeowners think about protecting. Unlike a driveway, a walkway does not carry vehicle weight, but it takes a steady beating from daily footsteps, snow shovels scraping the surface, and de-icing salt applied liberally to keep the path safe in winter.

All-Seal's walkway sealing gives these paths the same protection level as a driveway or patio, closing off the surface pores that let water in and set the stage for cracking, staining and moss growth.

Narrow walkways and paths are particularly susceptible to freeze-thaw cracking because they often have less mass and support underneath compared to a full driveway slab, and they typically run along the sides of a house where shade lingers longer. Water that seeps into unsealed concrete along a shaded path freezes overnight through a Southwestern Ontario winter and slowly widens any existing surface imperfection into a full crack. Sealing keeps that water from getting in in the first place.
Moss and algae in shaded sections

Paths that run along the north side of a house, under mature trees or through garden beds tend to stay damp far longer than open, sunny concrete. That constant dampness on unsealed concrete is exactly what moss and algae need to establish themselves, which not only looks unattractive but can make the path genuinely slippery when wet. Sealed concrete holds far less surface moisture, which makes it much harder for moss and algae to take hold along those shaded stretches.
Snow shovels and salt take their toll

Every winter, walkways get scraped repeatedly with metal shovel edges and doused with rock salt or calcium chloride to keep them safe for walking. That combination of physical abrasion and chemical exposure is hard on unsealed concrete, wearing down the surface finish and letting salt penetrate more easily with each pass of the shovel. A sealed walkway resists both the abrasion and the salt penetration far better, so the surface holds its finish through a full winter of shovelling.

body.text: Keeping colour consistent along the full path

A walkway that runs from full sun near the driveway into shade along the side of the house often weathers unevenly when left unsealed, with the sunnier sections fading faster than the shaded ones. Sealing the entire path at once evens out that exposure, so the walkway keeps a consistent colour and finish from one end to the other instead of showing a patchwork of wear.
Sealing garden paths and connecting walkways

Beyond the front entry walkway, many Southwestern Ontario properties have connecting paths to a side yard, garden, shed or backyard patio. These secondary paths are just as prone to freeze-thaw cracking and moss growth as the main walkway, and sealing them at the same time as your main path or patio is usually the most efficient way to protect the whole property in one visit.
Shaded and low-traffic paths are usually the first place moss and cracking show up. If your walkway runs along a north-facing wall or under trees, it is a strong candidate for sealing.

Many walkways include a small step up to a porch, a transition slab at a side door, or a short run of steps down to a basement entry, and these small sections tend to get overlooked in a general assessment of a property's concrete. They see just as much foot traffic and weather exposure as the main path, often more, since they are used every single time someone enters or leaves through that door. We include these transition points in every walkway sealing job rather than treating them as a separate line item, since leaving them unsealed defeats much of the purpose of protecting the rest of the path.
Best time to seal a walkway

Late spring through early fall works well for walkway sealing, once the concrete has dried out from spring rain and before the first frost. Sealing ahead of winter gives the path its best defence against the coming season of shovelling and salting.

faqs.q: Can you seal a walkway that already has moss on it?
faqs.a: Yes. We pressure wash the surface to remove existing moss and algae before sealing, and the sealed surface holds far less moisture afterward, making regrowth much less likely.

faqs.q: Does sealing help with snow shovel damage?
faqs.a: Sealing adds a protective layer that resists the abrasion of repeated shovel scraping and the salt exposure that comes with winter walkway maintenance, helping the surface hold its finish longer.

faqs.q: Will my walkway need to be closed off while it cures?
faqs.a: There is a cure period before the sealer is fully set, and we will give you exact timing so you know when it is safe to walk on regularly.

faqs.q: Can garden paths be sealed along with the main walkway?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is often the most efficient approach, since secondary paths face the same freeze-thaw and moss risks as the main walkway.

faqs.q: How long does walkway sealing last?
faqs.a: Most walkways hold their seal for 2 to 5 years depending on sun exposure, shovel use and how much salt is applied through the winter.

faqs.q: Does sealing help with uneven fading along a path?
faqs.a: Yes. Sealing the entire path in one application evens out UV exposure differences between sunny and shaded sections, keeping the colour more consistent end to end.
